title: Retiring From the Role of Family Peacemaker
script: Narrator: [honestly] For most of my adult life, I've been the one my parents call when they're not speaking to each other, expected to translate one's grievances into terms the other might accept.
Narrator: [reflective] I never applied for this role, exactly; it was simply assumed, perhaps because I was the calmest of the three siblings, or the one least likely to take sides.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Whatever the reason, by my twenties I had become fluent in de-escalation, capable of soothing an argument before either party had fully finished raising their voice.
Narrator: [honestly] What I didn't notice, for years, was how much of my own opinion I was suppressing in order to remain useful as a neutral party.
Narrator: [reflective] I rarely said what I actually thought, since taking a side, even a justified one, would have disqualified me from the role everyone had quietly assigned me.

Narrator: [honestly] The cost of that neutrality became clear during an argument last winter, when my mother accused me of always favoring my father, simply because I hadn't defended her loudly enough.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I realized then that mediating hadn't made me impartial; it had made me invisible, since nobody actually knew what I believed about any of it.
Narrator: [determined] So, for the first time, I told them both plainly that I would no longer relay messages between two adults perfectly capable of speaking to each other directly.
Narrator: [honestly] That announcement did not go over well. My mother called it abandonment, and my father, characteristically, said very little at all.
Narrator: [reflective] It's been six months now, and although they still argue occasionally, they've been forced to resolve things without routing every complaint through me first.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Our relationship, oddly, has improved since I stopped mediating, since I finally get to be their son rather than their translator.

Narrator: [peacefully] I still care deeply about their marriage, but I've learned that caring doesn't require absorbing every unresolved conflict between two people ultimately responsible for their own relationship.
Narrator: [with a small smile] These days, when they call to complain about each other, I still listen, but I no longer feel obligated to fix what was never actually mine to fix.
